articles.title: Mass outages in Sudan after RSF drones hit five power stations
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Sudan's Paramilitary Rapid Support Forces launched a coordinated drone attack Monday (October 26, 2026) against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country's east, a government official told AFP .

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref, and one in White Nile state, "resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states", the official said on condition of anonymity.
All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has since April 2023 been at war with its former ally, the RSF.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people, already facing the world's largest hunger crisis.
An AFP correspondent in Al-Jazira state reported the electricity had been out since 2 a.m. (0000 GMT).
Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao in Gedaref, said the power there had also been out since the same time.
"My son is diabetic; his insulin has to be stored in the fridge," he told AFP over the phone, scared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoils.
"We have no idea when the power will come back," he added.

Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past Paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams, compounding the suffering of nearly 20 million people facing extreme hunger.
Sudan's war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks from across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October alone, drone strikes killed over 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.
Africa's third-largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.

articles.title: Plant-based meat yields higher share of absorbable protein than traditional meat: study
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: While plant-derived kababs may still struggle to replicate the taste and texture of meat from a tandoori joint, they may contain relatively more protein in a form that the body can absorb, according to a study presented on Monday (October 26, 2026).

In a collaboration between the CSIR–Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (CSIR-IHBT), Palampur, and the Good Food Institute (GFI) India, a non-profit that promotes alternative proteins such as plant-based, fermentation-derived and cultivated meat, scientists investigated whether protein bioavailability (meaning protein in a form that’s nutritively useful to the body) of traditional meat was the same as that of plant-based meat.

Tests on five cooked plant-based products — two burger patties, a nugget and two seekh kebabs — showed higher bioavailability percentages than their chicken counterparts, according to the findings presented at a press conference on Monday (October 26). The plant-based kebabs scored 80.8% and 86.1% against 38.8% for chicken. The nugget scored 61.2% against 43.4%, and the patties recorded about 57% and 58% against 21.2%.

The findings do not mean plant-based meat is healthier, but only that they are nutritively comparable, as ‘healthier’ is a subjective term, Dr. Padma Ishwarya, senior scientist at GFI India, told The Hindu . “It’s too much of a vague term. It’s too broad a term…for health, we need to do further studies.”

The chicken products held more crude protein and released more amino acids, the building blocks of protein, during digestion, and Dr. Ishwarya said more products and samples would be tested in the next phase.

The work has not yet been published as a journal paper. “It is a report that is hosted on our website, but it is very much peer-reviewed,” Dr. Ishwarya said in a conversation with The Hindu . Two experts reviewed it, she said, and it was an overview and that detailed manuscripts would follow.

The team used an in vitro method that simulated digestion in a laboratory. Samples went through a two-minute salivary phase, then a stomach phase with digestive enzymes at pH 2 to 3, and then an intestinal phase. The method follows INFOGEST, an internationally harmonised protocol, Dr. Ishwarya said.

The team added an ultrafiltration membrane chosen to mimic the pore size of the human intestine. Whatever passed through the membrane was deemed bioavailable, and only free amino acids were measured. Each sample was adjusted to start with 40 milligrammes of protein.

Animal studies remain the gold standard, she said, but are tedious and require ethical clearances. The simulated method is faster and more reproducible. The team plans to conduct tests across laboratories next year so that NABL-accredited labs can use the method.

Plant-based meat, Dr. Ishwarya said, is made “specifically for biomimicking animal-derived meat”, unlike crisps or cereals, which are plant-based foods. It is made from soya, pea or wheat gluten, mostly soya, and shaped by extrusion, a process in which material is pushed through a die under heat and pressure. She said it contains no synthetic chemicals beyond ingredients such as spices and texturisers.

The study examined only protein. An earlier analysis in 2024 of about 120 products in the Indian market, she said, found that saturated fat and sodium levels were comparable to those in animal-derived products, leaving room for reduction. Plant-based products also supplied dietary fibre, which animal-derived products do not.

articles.title: Indian publishers contest Modi government’s privacy law
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: A group of 21 news publishers has challenged the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 , India’s privacy law, in court, arguing it would trample investigative work and let the government identify journalists’ sources, documents show.

Prime ​Minister Narendra Modi’s government announced the implementation of the law in 2025 to protect the digital personal data of ⁠users, raising compliance requirements for platforms like Meta and Google. The publishers have said that since media outlets were not exempt, the law was an invasion of press freedom.

Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having ‌a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) said in a confidential filing at the Supreme Court, reviewed by Reuters .

The October 6, 2026 lawsuit, being ‌reported for the first time and due to be heard on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), is the most high-profile challenge to the government’s privacy ‌law. ⁠Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had challenged it.

It also ⁠marks an unusual challenge to the government from businesses headed by Mr. Ambani and Mr. Adani, who Opposition parties allege are close to Mr. Modi and get favourable treatment — charges the businesses and the government vehemently deny.
DNPA and the media groups did not respond to requests for comment from Reuters , and neither did the IT Ministry.

The publishers are demanding that most of the ‌law’s contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, be quashed. They are arguing that the law could force a journalist to get prior consent from a person they want to investigate and force publishers to erase stories. They also say powers granted by the law to demand information could expose reporters’ sources.

The law would “render investigative journalism a benign and neutered recorder ‌of events,” the 698-page filing said. The provisions “constitute pre-censorship which is anathema to any democracy worth its name”.

The lawsuit ​comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Mr. Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have not done enough to scrutinise the Modi government.
India’s ranking in Reporters Without Borders’ World ⁠Press Freedom Index fell to 157 th out of 180 countries this year, from 140 th in 2014 — but the government rejects the rankings.

Modi government says it respects press freedom and says India, which has a “vibrant press and media ecosystem” of hundreds of newspapers and TV ‌channels, does not need validation from foreign bodies.

DNPA’s members include Mr. Ambani’s Network18 , which has seven digital news platforms, Mr. Adani’s NDTV and other marquee media groups, including The Hindu, the Indian Express and Times Internet , which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.

articles.title: The Hindu Group, Cancer Institute launch book on comprehensive cancer care
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The Hindu Group, in association with the Cancer Institute (WIA), Adyar, launched Cancer 360: Overview of Detection, Treatment, Palliation , a book examining cancer care from prevention and early detection to treatment, rehabilitation and palliative care. The book was launched at The Hindu office in Chennai.

N. Ram, director of The Hindu Group, launched the book alongside Suresh Nambath, editor of The Hindu . Mr. Ram handed over the first copy to E. Hemanth Raj, executive vice-chairman of Cancer Institute.

Speaking at the launch, Mr. Ram emphasised the importance of making advanced cancer care accessible and affordable. He highlighted the institute’s work in providing treatment to those who need it most and stressed the need to ensure that advances in cancer care reach patients facing barriers to treatment.

Dr. Hemanth Raj spoke about the need to translate advances in cancer research, much of which takes place in the West, into practical interventions in local settings. He also highlighted the institute’s charitable programmes, supported by donations, to help patients access treatment and facilities, and its plans to expand cancer care to reach more patients.
Arvind Krishnamurthy, professor of surgical oncology at Cancer Institute, stressed the need for continued research to improve cancer care and develop better treatments.

The book also addresses care beyond treatment. Mahalakshmi Rangabashyam Shetty, ENT surgeon and lecturer in the Department of Surgical Oncology at the institute, spoke about individualised treatment plans developed through multidisciplinary consultations. She also highlighted the need to tailor exercise and nutrition regimens to individual patients, alongside supportive services such as hospice care.

Surendran Veeraiah, professor and head of the Department of Regional Cancer Centre (RCTC), Cancer Institute, emphasised the importance of psychological support and allied services. He said the book could help make technical information on comprehensive cancer care accessible to more people.

The book features contributions from experts across oncology and allied disciplines. Its chapters cover multidisciplinary tumour boards, psychological care, onco-physiotherapy, palliative care, cancer research, speech and swallowing rehabilitation, early detection, precision treatment, pathology, nutrition and healthcare quality.
The book is available free of cost to The Hindu subscribers at https://www.thehindu.com/premium/ebook/

articles.title: Over 100 mills commence sugar production
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: As many as 107 sugar mills have commenced sugarcane crushing for the marketing season that started on October 1, 2026, according to the Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association.
Sugar mills in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and Uttar Pradesh have commenced crushing operations.

The previous sugar season that ended on September 30 closed with approximately 36 lakh tonnes of carryover stocks, providing a base for meeting domestic consumption requirements. As of 25 October 2026, sugar production during the current 2026–27 season had reached approximately four lakh tonnes, compared with just about 0.6 lakh tonnes on the corresponding date last year.

The Government has extended the duty-free raw sugar import window and introduced stockholding limits. These measures, together with available carryover stocks and the commencement of fresh production, contribute to ensuring adequate sugar availability for domestic consumption during the festive period, it said.

articles.title: Keralam plans Bill to regulate high treatment costs in private hospitals
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The Keralam government will introduce a Bill in the next Assembly session to regulate high medical treatment costs in private hospitals, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan told the Assembly on Monday (October 26, 2026).

He was responding to a question from Communist Party of India (Marxist) MLA K.N. Balagopal on the steps being taken by the government to regulate the trend of some major hospitals, in which global private equity firms now have big stakes, inflating treatment costs.

The Minister said the government agreed in principle to the need to regulate private hospitals, many of which were now under the management of foreign companies. He said that while the costs for treatment as well as room rents have increased drastically, insurance companies are at times refusing claims, causing difficulties to the common people.

Responding to another question, Mr. Muraleedharan said the government was preparing a project to transform Keralam into a health destination which will be sought after by foreigners as well as those from other States. The Principal Secretary (Health department), Director of the Health Department and the Director of Medical Education will coordinate these activities.

A major campaign for early detection and control of lifestyle diseases is also underway. As part of this, heath workers will visit houses and identify those needing attention through a survey and preliminary screening. The pilot project will be implemented in the Vattiyurkavu, Idukki and Nilambur Assembly constituencies first and later expanded across the State, said Mr. Muraleedharan.

articles.title: Dubious retreat: on the National Medical Commission and its MSMER
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations. MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations. MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.
• Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

articles.title: A final surge: on Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s triumph in Brazil
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

Core Context & Background: Nayara Energy, India's largest private fuel retailer, has raised petrol prices by ₹5 per litre and diesel by ₹3 with immediate effect, seeking to narrow the gap between retail prices and rising international oil and refined-product costs, people familiar with the matter said.

2. Key Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The latest increase comes amid renewed pressure on fuel retailers from higher global energy prices and follows a series of price adjustments by Nayara this year as refiners grapple with the impact of geopolitical disruptions on crude and product markets. Nayara, which operates 7,108 petrol pumps across the country, raised petrol and diesel prices with effect from early hours of Saturday (October 3, 2026), sources said.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: On October 1, the government said private retailers should not cap petrol and diesel sales at their outlets, after Nayara and Jio-bp restricted volumes at some pumps amid losses on retail sales.

1. Core Context & Background: The story so far: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 , to permit the use of ethanol-based fuels containing up to 100% ethanol (E100) in vehicles.

2. Key Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The move paves the way for flex-fuel vehicles, which can run on petrol, ethanol blends of varying proportions, or pure ethanol. The amendments modify Rule 115, which deals with emission standards and related requirements for motor vehicles, and Rule 115E, which contains additional provisions relating to emission testing.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: These concerns have prompted calls for a transparent assessment.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: India is poised to strengthen its position as a global refining hub, with its oil processing capacity set to rise to 300 million tonnes annually by 2030 even as Europe and other parts of the Western world see refinery capacity decline, Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

2. Key Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: India's refining capacity is currently around 290 million tonnes per annum and is expected to expand further by scaling up existing facilities and adding new projects, the Union Petroleum Minister said at a news conference on the sidelines of the 29th Energy Technology and Innovation Meet in south Goa. He said the expansion will allow India not only to meet its domestic energy requirements but also to supply more petroleum products to international markets.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: "Beyond conventional petroleum products, initiatives such as Samudra Manthan and GOBARdhan (Galvanising Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan) are also expected to gain momentum, he said, adding that these developments would complement the country's expanding energy infrastructure.
